subject: Trees killed inadvertently
comment: This is so very sad, and unfortunate. You need to deal with this problem right away. If trees on the west side are a priority, they should be replaced, now.. Or at least in the fall. I imagine finding enough trees and ordering them might take a while. And, you should compensate for the fact that the trees already had some growth on them. Do not buy small trees. Buy larger trees, so the canopy will get bigger sooner. You need to have some sort of educational program to teach the people who have a new tree the proper watering procedure. And, you should have someone from the city driving around for a couple of years to make sure that the trees are properly watered. I know you do this already, but not sure what your criteria is for which trees get extra water. They should have those green bags around them, and the driver can make sure they are properly filled. That same driver can remove the bag once they have been on the tree long enough so they don't cause damage. Now is the time to show the people of the city, and especially the West side, that you really have a good tree canopy as a priority, that you aren't just blowing smoke. You can find the money somewhere. Do this now and get publicity for it. Thank you for your quick attention to this matter. Judi Short

subject: ... just trust me, "it really does work"
comment: Hi All, In my search for folks and organizations who are concerned about the number of mentally ill and addicted folks sleeping on our streets, something interesting is happening. It seems many of those who are "concerned" and are "dedicated" and advocate for more and more funding, seem to be the most resistant to finding out what really does or does not work. The article in this morning's Tribune about the snake oil salesman whose pitch was "Silver is the solution", "trust me" when it came to having a treatment for Covid was interesting. When there is no known solution to a problem, we humans are free to create one, and then pretend and convince ourselves and others that our solution really works, even if it doesn't. Interesting, but it is what we do. We then promote what we have created and charge as much as we can for it. Three local homeless and mental health service providers I approached have said, "come to us, we can help you", "trust me", but they have absolutely no data that suggests their solutions work any better than the silver stuff the guy in the article was pushing. And all three offer advice to decision makers and are instrumental in referring people to or offering treatments. And what really troubles me, when asked about the need for data, all three said that too much data would only confuse things and make it harder to "help people". So what are we to do. Pretend and promote ... or search for answers that could really help people with whatever their problem is. If in the process of searching for something that really works, we might consider funding only programs that can prove they actually help people. This simple action will drive the silver selling folks out of business. Funding "silver is the solution" type programs and treatment efforts helps no one. I think, no, I know we can do better. Bernie Hart Salt Lake City, Ut

subject: Additional increase of city council's salary
comment: Dear City Councilors: As a citizen and a tax payer of Salt Lake City, I would like to give my thoughts on the suggested additional salary increase of the city council. I do not support any additional raise of your salary at this time. Here are my thoughts I want to share with you: First, it's not our job to consider a candidate's personal wealth or employment status when someone runs for the office, We can only trust whoever runs for the office can work effectively with or without any other job(s) they may have. All the candidates know what they are getting into when they run, and we hope the motive to run is the desire to serve the community, rather than money, authority, fame, or even career. Second, if I apply for a $50,000 job, that's what I expect to be paid even if I have to work overtime sometimes. That's how salary works. A raise is given for the job well done, with a consideration of how well the company has done and what it can afford. It's not something I give myself because I feel entitled to it. Third, number of hours someone works for doesn't always equal how well the job gets done. A skilled worker can get the same job done more quickly and efficiently than an unskilled or distracted worker, for example. So why should an unskilled or distracted worker get paid more based on how many hours it has taken? (I'm not implying any of you being an unskilled worker.) Fourth, by giving yourselves another raise*, you will be taking funds away from something else. Are those funds something you didn't need in the first place? Less amount was adequate? Then why do you keep increasing utilities, fees, and taxes? Taking my money to fatten your wallet? (* However you call it, I consider it a raise. You want to "correct ordinance?" Why not put it on the table first? Can city council change any ordinances anytime without anyone's consent?) My hope is that you will set aside the feelings of entitlement, ego, and superiority to the people you serve and remember why you ran for the office. I hope you remember the people you are serving are paying your salary. There are many residents, especially on the west side, who work hard full time but don't even make as much as you make part time. The median household income in Rose Park is $57,620. Your job is part time, and I hope it will stay that way rather than creating a lot of career politicians. If you don't think you are not compensated enough for what you do, maybe this is not the right job for you. Thanks for reading, Keiko Jones District 3 Resident of Fairpark Community

subject: Stabilization fee
comment: Hello Dan, As a constituent of District 6, a devoted resident of Salt Lake City, and a former city employee, I try to stay informed about what is happening in and around Salt Lake City. I was surprised to receive a SLC Public Utilities bill for July that was double the amount I normally pay. I traced my payments for June, May and April of this year by way of comparison. Looking closely at statements from past months, I noticed the Stabilization Fee was a new fee in July and called the Public Utilities office to learn that City Council had passed this fee (effective July 1) to stabilize costs for water usage since payments for water have been lower with successful conservation efforts and revenue to the city must be stabilized. I xeriscaped my yard 4 years ago for low water usage. I water my yard once a week from June through September. I am a single household and watch my water usage carefully. So I'm trying to understand why my public utilities bill will now be $40 more a month (nearly $500 for the year) when I've made every effort to conserve! Besides this not being anything for which I have budgeted, logically, I wonder why conservation isn't acknowledged rather than throwing on an additional fee? With this $40 a month in new fees and the recent tax increase that is scheduled for the downtown Sports and Entertainment district, I'm certain you are driving devoted and long-standing SLC residents to reconsider living within city limits. Please offer any reasonable explanation why every household is now absorbing an additional public utilities fee, especially when we are encouraged to conserve water, and do let me know if this is something that you voted in favor of? I appreciate your public service and look forward to a reply. Thank you. Kind Regards, -Alison McFarlane

subject: Support for Rio Grande Plan
comment: Dear Councilman Dugan, I am writing to ask that you support Salt Lake City's Rio Grande Proposal. This proposal would greatly improve our state by removing several dangerous railroad crossings (including 200S, 800S and 900S to name a few) and opening over 70 acres for development. This project would improve the experience of commuters and long-distance travelers, all while helping to begin the healing of the east-west divide in Salt Lake City. A new central station located at the Rio Grande Depot would be a strong welcome to those who travel to Utah via train. It would provide significantly more amenities than the existing Salt Lake Central Station, all while being closer to downtown. The Rio Grande Plan proposes the relocation of the tracks into a "Train Box" along 500 West. This Train Box would be a shallow tunnel wide enough for up to six train tracks allowing for all connections to the current system to be maintained and expanded. Our city prepared for the 2002 Olympics by cutting back the freeway viaducts to where they are today, the Rio Grande Plan would allow these ramps to be shortened once more, opening up valuable street frontage. The estimated price tag of this project is similar to UDOT's I-15 widening between Farmington and Salt Lake City, making the Rio Grande Plan an ideal project to complete before the Olympics. If this project were pursued as an Olympic transportation infrastructure project it would likely receive significant federal funding to reduce the burden on Utah's taxpayers. The transportation legacy of the 2002 Winter Olympics are the billions of dollars of freeway projects completed leading up to the games. Most of the 2002 Olympic freeway improvements are still serving Utah well, allowing for transit projects such as The Rio Grande Proposal to be a focus in 2034. As the state continues to expand, we need to be looking for more sustainable development. I believe the Rio Grande Plan would help us build a more sustainable Utah. Expanding the freeways would result in increased traffic and pollution from the volume of cars on the road, a rising heat index from the concrete and asphalt structures absorbing heat, and decreased walkability, access to public transit, and dependence on cars in an already congested state. It's been proven repeatedly that expanding freeways doesn't alleviate traffic, and I don't feel that Utah should be putting valuable time and resources into something that wouldn't benefit the residents. Please show your support for the Rio Grande plan, which would continue to benefit Utah for generations to come. Thanks, Marisa Lee Salt Lake City, UT

subject: Public Utilities bill
comment: Councilperson Dugan, I am in receipt today of my new Public Utilities bill. I am not clear on what role you get to play in the remarkable increases in the various rates, but please count me as appalled. Of particular concern are the following: The franchise fee is now 2.97 times the amount on the immediate prior bill – that is a 197% increase! My new bill shows a "stabilization fee" of $21.21 for the sewer, which had never been part of the sewer charges before, and effectively increases the sewer rate by 80%. Excluding the "stabilization fee" added to the water portion, referenced following, the effective charge per gallon of water increased 24.2%. The new "stabilization fee" of $20.43 has been added to my water bill, and when compared to the total water bill of last month, was equal to 22% of the total charge for water. The charge for street lights increased 21%, although I must note that I pay for the maintenance and electricity for the street light on my property on Devonshire – not reimbursed by the City's charge, as do all of the others with street lights on their property on Devonshire – there is not a city-provided street light in the area. The daily charge for my 40 gallon garbage container increased 10% – not unreasonable, when compared to all of the above. I do remember having received notice of the proposed increase in garbage fees, but if there were a notice of all of the suddenly-new stabilization fees and the enormous increase in the franchise fee, it failed to reach me. Was there actually notice of those new fees and the other significant increases? If not, was the omission of such notice deliberate, to avoid a public outcry? For us, as your constituents here in District 6, we must see you as responsible to us for these increases, since we cannot vote for councilpersons in the other districts or City employees. And I suppose, since these are all deemed "purchases" in the City, once the "support the billionaires" one-half percent additional tax is added, it will increase my bill further. Once again, I am appalled. Please advise. Joan Ogden
